CLERK'S NOTICE SETTING PRE-SETTLEMENT CONFERENCE MEETING VIA ZOOM AUDIO CONFERENCE. Notice is hereby given to all parties that Magistrate Judge Lisa J. Cisneros will convene a telephonic pre-settlement conference to discuss timing and preparation for the settlement conference. Judge Cisneros anticipates that the phone call will last approximately 15-30 minutes. Lead Counsel for all parties shall participate.The conference all shall take place on January 9, 2025 and 10:30 a.m. using Judge Cisneros's designated non-public Zoom Audio Conference. You will initially enter a "waiting room" and will be admitted into the meeting by court staff. The parties will receive an email from Judge Cisneros's Courtroom Deputy the day before the call with the call-in information. If counsel for either side is not available for the above date they must meet and confer with the other side and send an email to Judge Cisneros's CRD, Brittany Sims at ljccrd@cand.uscourts.gov providing a new date(s) to the Court within three business days. The parties are directed to review, in advance of the telephone pre-settlement conference Judge Cisneros's Settlement Standing Order on Judge Cisneros's webpage, by going to https://www.cand.uscourts.gov/wp-content/uploads/judges/cisneros-ljc/LJC-SettlementConferenceStandingOrder.pdf (This is a text-only entry generated by the court.    QUESTION 2. Capital One installed third-party code on its website that sent Plaintiffs’
 1 personal and financial information to third parties in real-time.

 2
               Plaintiffs start with Question 2 because Capital One must establish its data collection
 3
     practice before it can establish that its actions fall within the scope of its disclosures or that
 4
     Plaintiffs consented to the practice. Calhoun v. Google, LLC, 113 F.4th 1141, 1147 (9th Cir. 2024)
 5

 6 (holding consent “is only effective if the person alleging harm consented ‘to the particular conduct,

 7 or to substantially the same conduct’ and if the alleged tortfeasor did not exceed the scope of that

 8 consent.”) (internal citation omitted).

 9             Capital One installed third-party code on its website that runs as if it is Capital One’s own
10
     website code. ECF 1 at ¶¶ 1, 44. When a user visits Capital One’s website, the third-party’s code
11
     installs pieces of code (“tags”) on the user’s computer that act like computer viruses – they tell the
12
     customer’s computer what to do and steal data about the user and their interactions on Capital
13

14 One’s website, including: employment and bank account information; citizenship status; user’s

15 eligibility, pre-approval, or credit card approval; identifying information like IP addresses and

16 “cookies”; and browsing activity. Id. ¶¶ 41-42, 45, 47, 52-59, 60, 65-71, 187. The tags

17
     “instantaneously and surreptitiously duplicate communications” between the user and Capital
18
     One’s website and “send them to the third-party” (like Facebook) that created the tag. Id. ¶¶ 42,
19
     47, 64.
20
               The code on Capital One’s website thus allows third parties to steal personal information
21

22 directly from the user’s browser and Capital One’s server in real-time. Id. ¶ 43. If a customer clicks

23 a button, it instantaneously triggers the tags to begin transmitting user data. A user cannot detect,

24 delete, or opt-out of the tags or their data transmission. Id. ¶¶ 43, 140-42. Tags enable third parties

25
     to use the stolen data to find customers, drive sales via targeted ads, and assess ad impact. Id. ¶ 49.
26
27

   QUESTION 1. The Online Privacy Policy does not disclose the extent of the collection or use
 1 of Plaintiffs’ Personal Information.

 2
            The Policy states: “We and our third-party providers may collect information about your
 3
     activities on our Online Services and across different websites, mobile apps, and devices over time
 4
     for targeted advertising purposes.” ECF 1-2 at 7 (emphasis added). A “‘reasonable’ user … with
 5

 6 the level of sophistication attributable to the general public,” would not understand this vague

 7 disclosure to mean: (1) that Capital One may share the user’s personal and financial information

 8 with third parties, nor (2) that Capital One shares such information with third parties regardless of

 9 whether the third party acts on Capital One’s behalf. Calhoun, 113 F.4th at 1147.

10
            First, Capital One’s Online Privacy Policy states that information about a user’s “activities”
11
     on the website may be shared but offers no explanation of what “activities” means. A reasonable
12
     user may understand some general information, like the fact that they visited a Capital One
13

14 website, is shared with Capital One providers to service ads on Capital One’s website. They would

15 not, however, understand this vague disclosure to mean that Capital One shares all manner of their

16 private and financial information—including credit card application information, employment

17
     information, and bank account information—with undisclosed third parties, whom in turn may
18
     share it with undisclosed fourth parties for marketing and sales purposes. ECF 1 at ¶ 47.
19
            Second, the Policy’s disclosure states that activity information may be shared with “our”
20
     (i.e., Capital One’s) “third-party providers,” meaning providers that advertise for Capital One.
21

22 ECF 1-2 at 7. Earlier language in the section clarifies: “[Capital One] and third-party providers

23 acting on our behalf use online tracking technology to conduct . . . targeted advertising.” Id.

24 (emphasis added). The section further specifies that “our advertising providers” may use Plaintiffs’

25
     information to advertise on non-Capital One websites, but only for “Capital One ad[s].” Id. at 7
26
     (emphasis added). The only reasonable interpretation of these disclosures is that information may
27
                      PLAINTIFFS’ RESPONSES TO QUESTIONS FOR HEARING
                                     Case No. 3:24-cv-05985
                                                2
              Case 3:24-cv-05985-TLT           Document 56        Filed 01/20/25       Page 4 of 6




     be shared with advertisers to promote Capital One’s products—not that information is shared with
 1

 2 unknown third and fourth parties to market third- and fourth-party products. ECF 1 at ¶¶ 47, 49,

 3 118, 132. Because Capital One’s sharing exceeds the scope of this provision, it cannot show that

 4 Plaintiffs consented to the disclosure of their personal information. Calhoun, 113 F.4th at 1147.

 5
     QUESTION 3. Capital One’s disclosure of financial information involves a property interest.
 6
            This District repeatedly has found that plaintiffs have a property interest in their personal,
 7
     financial, and online data sufficient to confer standing under the UCL. E.g., In re Meta Pixel Tax
 8
     Filing Cases, 724 F. Supp. 3d 987, 1024-25 (N.D. Cal. 2024) (collection and sharing of name,
 9

10 email addresses, income, tax filing status, tax refund amounts, and dependents’ college scholarship

11 amounts constitute injury to “present or future property interest”); Brown v. Google LLC, 2021 WL

12 6064009, at *2-3, *15 (N.D. Cal. Dec. 22, 2021) (collection and sale of data including IP addresses,

13 browser history, and URL information “‘diminished’ Plaintiffs’ ‘future property interest’” under

14
     UCL) (citation omitted); Calhoun v. Google LLC, 526 F. Supp. 3d 605, 613-14, 635-36 (N.D. Cal.
15
     2021) (similar); A.B. ex rel. v. Google LLC, 737 F. Supp. 3d 869, 881-82 (N.D. Cal. 2024)
16
     (plaintiffs had property interest in data and UCL standing where collected data included device
17

18 identifiers, location, app usage, in-app behavior, and cookies); Stark v. Patreon, Inc., 635 F. Supp.
19 3d 841, 854 (N.D. Cal. 2022) (plaintiffs “lost property” when personal information was disclosed);

20 Kis v. Cognism Inc., 2024 WL 3924553, at *2 (N.D. Cal., Aug. 23, 2024) (plaintiff had property

21
     interest in name, contact information, job title, place of work, and location); see also Griffith v.
22
     Tiktok, Inc., 697 F.Supp.3d 963, 967 (C.D. Cal. 2023) (recognizing “property interest” and UCL
23
     standing in data like user ID, email, IP address, browser histories, search queries, and screen
24
     resolution). Similarly, here, Plaintiffs identify “several ways to conceptualize the[ir] . . . injuries
25

26 as injuries to money or property.” Meta Pixel, 724 F. Supp. 3d at 1024. Defendant’s motion fails.
